traces.name: mock_game-of-24
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: All six operations, including simulation: the tree descends greedily by value, in the real environment, until one number is left. Solved on the fifth iteration, after four dead ends.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24_no-value
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: Ablation: lambda = 0, so V(s) is self-consistency alone and the value function's grade is thrown away. A solution does turn up - built during a rollout on the first iteration - but selection never walks back into it, so all twelve iterations back up a reward of 0.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24_greedy
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: Ablation: w = 0, so UCT collapses to pure exploitation. It starves the branch that wins: the answer opens on a fraction, which the policy scores badly, and without the exploration bonus that branch stays the least visited of the five. Never finds 24.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24_react
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: ReAct on the same puzzle: one sample per step, taken without comparison. It opens with 2 / 8 - the first move LATS needed five iterations to settle on - then takes 5 - 11 and ends at -24. One trajectory, and no way back into it.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24_reflexion
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: Reflexion: twelve ReAct trials, a note after each failure. Trial 1 opens with 2 / 8, goes wrong a step later, and its note says not to open with that step again - blaming the one move that was right. No later trial opens with it, and all twelve fail. A note blames a whole trajectory; in LATS the value of 2 / 8 is an average over every rollout through it, so one bad continuation does not condemn the opening.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24_tot
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: Tree of Thoughts with a beam of two. Of the five openings it draws, only 2 / 8 can still reach 24, and the policy grades that fraction 0.15 - so the first cut keeps 5 - 2 (0.9) and 2 * 5 (0.7) and drops it for good. The beam ends three tidy steps later at 1. LATS gives 2 / 8 the same low first value; the exploration bonus is what brings it back.

traces.name: openai_game-of-24
traces.title: Game of 24
traces.note: gpt-5 on the easy puzzle, and the honest counterexample: a strong policy needs no search. The five root samples split three to two between 8 / 2 and 11 - 5, and the grader, reading the numbers each move left, gives both 0.98 - both can still reach 24 - so self-consistency breaks the tie, 0.79 to 0.69. Every later sample is unanimous, five of five, and the first rollout scores 1: seven requests in all. Read it next to mock_game-of-24, which needs five iterations and forty-five nodes to reach the same place.

traces.name: mock_merge-intervals
traces.title: Merge intervals
traces.note: The programming setting: every node is a complete program, its reward is the fraction of tests it passes, and simulation is skipped. Before anything runs the model prefers the one-pass sweep, 0.70 to 0.62; once the tests have run the grader reads 3 of 5 against 4 of 5 and the order flips. Exploration still spends iteration 2 on the one-pass branch, where every patch caps at three of five, and iteration 3 solves it from sort-then-sweep.

traces.name: mock_merge-intervals_value-before
traces.title: Merge intervals
traces.note: Ablation, and the old behaviour: LM(s) is the model's grade from before the tests ran - the ordering Tree of Thoughts uses, and what version 1.0 of this generator did on every trace. The one-pass sweep wins the first evaluation on opinion alone and is backed up at 0.6, and exploration rather than the value carries iteration 2 to the right branch. Both runs reach 5 of 5; what differs is what V(s) means - here what the model expected, beside it what the tests said.

traces.name: mock_merge-intervals_react
traces.title: Merge intervals
traces.note: ReAct: one program, then one patch of it. It writes the model's favourite, the one-pass sweep, patches it with the model's favourite fix, and stops at 3 of 5. The approach was the bug, and ReAct never sees an alternative to it.

traces.name: mock_merge-intervals_reflexion
traces.title: Merge intervals
traces.note: Reflexion: trial 1 is the ReAct run, 3 of 5. Its note reads the failures - every failing case arrives out of order - and says sort first. Trial 2 opens with sort-then-sweep and patches it to 5 of 5. On this task one well-aimed note does the work of the whole tree.

traces.name: mock_merge-intervals_tot
traces.title: Merge intervals
traces.note: Tree of Thoughts, beam of two, valued by the model's opinion alone. At depth 2 it writes the correct program - merge on touch too, 5 of 5 - grades it 0.64, and drops it for two patches it likes more, 0.78 and 0.71. It returns a program that passes 3 of 5. The tests were run on every program and read for none.

traces.name: mock_multihop-qa
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: Two-hop retrieval with a distractor. A grader that counts words cannot tell the UCT page from the page that holds the answer - 0.59 each - and the first rollout opens with the distractor. The answer it then tries twice, ECML 2006, comes straight back rejected both times, so the rollout runs out of depth rather than committing to it. Iteration 2 starts from the right page, and the policy's recency bias now points at the right venue.

traces.name: mock_multihop-qa_no-reflection
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: Ablation: reflection off. Identical outcome, one step shorter - which is the paper's own finding. Reflection is the smallest of its three ablations; the value function and the search structure matter more.

traces.name: mock_multihop-qa_react
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: ReAct: it reads the distractor, then the page that holds the answer, and answers from the distractor - ECML 2006. One sample per step, so a single draw of the policy's bias decides it, and nothing gets a second look.

traces.name: mock_multihop-qa_reflexion
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: Reflexion: eight trials, eight failures. Every note is accurate - each names the wrong answer and the page it came from - and none says where to look, so each trial learns one more answer not to give and wanders the corpus again. With no value function, nothing carries over about which states were promising.

traces.name: mock_multihop-qa_tot
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: Tree of Thoughts: by depth four it has written the right answer and two wrong ones, and the model is exactly as sure of Computers and Games 2006 as of EMNLP 2023 - 0.85 each. With nothing from the environment to separate them, it returns the one it found first, which is wrong.

traces.name: openai_multihop-qa
traces.title: Two-hop question answering
traces.note: gpt-5 on two-hop retrieval, and what self-consistency means for a real model. Each step's three samples are worded differently - eight distinct strings in the whole run - but they agree on what they do: the same page, then the same page again, then the same answer. Agreement is counted on that, not on the wording, so every level is one child with SC(s) = 1. The grader marks the first page down to 0.22, since it names the algorithm but not where it was introduced, and the second up to 0.99; the first trajectory is accepted. Six requests. mock_multihop-qa is where the loop has something to do.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24-hard
traces.title: Game of 24, the hard one
traces.note: 6, 9, 9, 10, where the twelve best-looking first moves are all dead ends and every solution ends in 9 + 15. On this seed the offline policy, which rates a fraction badly, never proposes a move that reaches 15, so sixteen iterations of correct search find nothing. Search cannot choose what the policy never suggests - compare the Reflexion run, and the OpenAI runs, on the same puzzle.

traces.name: mock_game-of-24-hard_reflexion
traces.title: Game of 24, the hard one
traces.note: A seed on which starting over beats searching: Reflexion solves the puzzle on its fifth trial, and the LATS run on the same seed never does. LATS expanded the root once and searched the five moves it drew there. Reflexion starts again every trial, each note forbids the opening that just failed, and trial 5 opens with 6 / 10 - a fraction no tidy-minded policy picks first - then 9 / 3/5 = 15 and 9 + 15 = 24. Over sixty seeds LATS still solves this puzzle more often, 17 to 10; the README has the table.

traces.name: openai_game-of-24-hard
traces.title: Game of 24, the hard one
traces.note: gpt-5 on the hard puzzle, and the clearest case in the set for grading after the reply. Five independent samples reach four openings. The policy's own priors favour 9 / 9 and 10 - 9 at 0.95; the grading call, which sees the numbers each move left, gives them 0.12 and 0.06 - nothing makes 24 from 1, 6, 10 or 1, 6, 9 - and gives 9 / 6 0.98, because 10 * 3/2 = 15 and 15 + 9 = 24. It is the only one of the four that can reach 24, one sample in five proposed it, and the first rollout takes it: solved in one iteration, nine requests. With the priors in V(s) instead, 9 / 9 would have led that rollout into a dead end.

traces.name: openai_game-of-24-hard_wide
traces.title: Game of 24, the hard one
traces.note: gpt-5 on the hard puzzle with twelve samples instead of five, and the case against trusting agreement alone. Half the samples agree on 10 - 9, the move the policy also rates highest (prior 0.93); it is a dead end - nothing makes 24 from 1, 6, 9 - and the grading call, which sees those numbers, gives it 0.0. 10 / 6, proposed twice, gets 0.96, because 9 * 5/3 = 15 and 15 + 9 = 24. V(s) ranks it first, 0.56 to 0.25, where self-consistency alone or the priors would have rolled out 10 - 9. Solved on the first rollout, in twelve requests: gpt-5 takes at most eight samples per request, so each expansion is two.
